newsitem.title: ETHIOPIA: One dead, 42 hurt in Ethiopia grenade blasts.
newsitem.headline: One dead, 42 hurt in Ethiopia grenade blasts.

text.p: Grenade attacks in the Ethiopian capital killed at least one person and wounded 42 including four Britons and a French couple, diplomats and state radio reported on Sunday.
Two British men wounded in one blast on Saturday night said they were in Ethiopia to train the police and threw themselves on top of one of the grenades to protect their wives.
They were sitting down for a meal at Blue Tops, an expensive Italian restaurant favoured by foreigners and rich Ethiopians.

Ethiopian radio said at least one person was killed and 34 were wounded when a grenade was lobbed into the Tigray Hotel near the busy Piazza area in the city centre, at about the same time as the attack on Blue Tops. The identity of the person killed was not immediately known.
The blasts appeared to be the latest in a series of politically motivated bombings in Addis Ababa and provincial cities. State radio did not say if any suspects had been arrested.

President Meles Zenawi's government blamed Moslem fundamentalists for a wave of bomb attacks last year in the capital and in the east. Ethiopian authorities remain secretive about their investigations into the bombings.
Diplomats said they had unconfirmed reports of at least two more grenade attacks in Addis Ababa on Saturday night but that one of the devices failed to explode.
"The two British men were reasonably seriously injured, mostly from flying glass. But their wives are not too bad and none of their lives is in danger," British consul Florence Napthen said.

Britons John Bown and Blair Davies told Reuters in the Black Lion hospital that as they sat down to dine, they saw something that looked like an explosive device being lobbed near their table. They threw themselves on the device to protect their wives, suffering multiple lacerations.
British embassy spokeswoman Janet Duff said there was no evidence so far to suggest the two men were deliberately targeted because they were training the police.
British, French and German tourists were wounded last February in a grenade attack on a hotel in the ancient walled city of Harar in the east.
Last November, hijackers believed to be Ethiopians seized an Ethiopian Airlines plane and forced it to ditch into the sea off the Comoro Islands, killing 125 people on board.

The manager of Blue Tops, Luigi Ferrari, told Reuters three men entered the restaurant at about 7.40 p.m. and after a brief conversation with a waitress lobbed two grenades at the eight diners inside.

"Two Jamaicans were untouched but two British couples and a French couple were all injured. I believe the French lady was the most seriously hurt and lost one eye from the shrapnel," Ferrari told Reuters.
"We were lucky that it was early because we were fully booked from 8.30," he said.
Ferrari and other sources said the French couple were taken to the Russian-run Baltcha hospital.
Last August Ethiopian troops backed by the air force raided western Somalia to strike at alleged bases of Moslem fundamentalists. The Horn of Africa country has both Christian and Moslem populations.

The government has bad relations with neighbouring Sudan and accused Khartoum of helping to plot the failed assassination attempt against Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak when he visited Addis Ababa in June 1995.
